strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulations: the Reach-Always-Avoid (RAA) and Reach-Reach (RR) problems naturally generalize prior reach/avoid/reach-avoid HJ-RL formulations to dual-objective satisfaction with a worst-case (min) composition, filling a real gap between CMDPs, multi-objective RL, and temporal-logic approaches.

Substantial theoretical contribution: Theorems 1-3, with complete and careful proofs in the supplementary material (including the counterexample in Fig. 2 showing non-augmented memoryless policies are fundamentally insufficient), establish exact value decompositions into reach, avoid, and reach-avoid problems, plus Bellman equations and an optimality result for the state augmentation.

The proposed DO-HJ-PPO algorithm is a principled extension of the Stochastic Reach(-Avoid) Bellman Equation machinery of [21], including a policy-gradient result (Prop. 1) and reach-avoid GAEs, with implementation details (hyperparameters, coupled resets) provided for reproducibility.

Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over reasonable baselines (CPPO variants, decomposed STL) on Hopper and F16 continuous-control tasks in both success rate and steps-to-success, plus a clean DDQN grid-world verification of the theory.

Good positioning relative to related work (CMDPs, multi-objective RL, goal-conditioned RL, STL/LTL RL), clearly articulating why explicit Bellman forms avoid reward engineering and surrogate-automaton issues.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: the paper closely builds on [18, 19, 21] (RABE/SRBE and the PPO-based reach-avoid algorithm of So et al.); the main contribution is composing two known subproblem types, and the practical algorithm differs from the prior PPO recipe mainly by extra critic networks and modified rewards.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only two environment families (Hopper, F16) with one grid-world demonstration; no learning curves across seeds, no statistical significance reporting in the main text, and no ablation beyond the qualitative statement about coupled resets.

A theory-practice gap is acknowledged but not analyzed: the decomposition results assume deterministic dynamics, finite state/action spaces, and access to pre-solved decomposed values, whereas the algorithm jointly learns decomposed values in continuous stochastic settings; the effect of these relaxations on guarantees is not quantified.

Baselines are somewhat ad hoc: CPPO is acknowledged not to be designed for max/min accumulated objectives, and the multiple hand-crafted CPPO variants (v1-v3) make the comparison feel tuned; no comparison against more direct multi-objective or non-Markovian-reward baselines (e.g., reward machines).
The augmented state space depends on the range of reward/penalty values, which may scale poorly with rich reward functions; practical implications of this scaling are not discussed.

Writing has minor issues (e.g., typos such as 'reach-aviod', 'solitons', 'to incentive'), and the main text is terse, requiring frequent reference to the supplementary material for key algorithmic details.

strengths: The core theoretical contribution is clean and rigorous: the decomposition results (Theorems 1 and 2) that reduce the RAA and RR problems to compositions of previously studied reach, avoid, and reach-avoid Bellman equations are non-trivial, and the supplementary proofs are detailed and appear correct.

Theorem 3 convincingly establishes that the proposed state augmentation is optimal in the sense that no additional history information (or stochasticity) can improve performance, which is an important sanity check given the non-Markovian nature of the objectives.
The paper correctly identifies that max/min-over-time objectives (unlike plain reach/avoid) require history-dependent policies, and the grid-world example in Figure 2 illustrates this well.

DO-HJ-PPO is a sensible algorithmic realization of the theory, and the experiments (DDQN grid-world, Hopper, F16) qualitatively demonstrate behavior (visiting both targets, avoiding hazards before and after reaching) that simple reach/avoid baselines cannot express.
Hyperparameters and baseline formulations are documented in detail in the supplementary material, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work: the paper is essentially a direct generalization of the Reach-Avoid Bellman equation (Hsu et al., 2021) and the Stochastic Reachability Bellman Equation/PPO (So et al., 2024) to two specific two-objective compositions. The overall recipe (compose lower-level Bellman problems) is foreshadowed by those works, and the 'road-map' claim toward arbitrary higher-level problems is vague and unsupported.

There is a substantial gap between the exact theory and the proposed algorithm. Theorems 1-2 assume exact, deterministic values (e.g., r_RAA depends on the precomputed optimal avoid value V*_A), whereas DO-HJ-PPO uses on-policy learned critic estimates in a nonstationary modified reward. No convergence analysis or error analysis of this approximation is provided, so the central optimality guarantees do not directly transfer to the practical method.

Evaluation is narrow and baselines are weak. Only two continuous environments (Hopper, F16) plus a toy grid-world are considered. The main baselines (CPPO variants) are acknowledged adaptations not designed for max/min accumulated objectives, and the DSTL baseline is described as naive; stronger multi-objective RL, STL/TL-based, or reward-machine baselines are not compared. Results are reported only as bar charts of success percentage and mean steps, with limited statistical detail (seeds, variance, learning curves).

The problem class itself is quite restricted: conjunctions of two threshold-style objectives expressible with max/min over time. The relationship to STL/LTL fragments is not deeply explored despite the framing, and the claim of a general decomposition methodology is not substantiated beyond the two cases studied.

Writing quality issues undermine polish: repeated typos ('reach-aviod', 'contrained', 'incentive', 'solitons'), a likely typo in the statement of Theorem 2 (left-hand side written as V_RAA instead of V_RR), and occasional inconsistent notation. These are concerning in a theory-heavy paper.

Several technical assumptions limit generality: deterministic dynamics, deterministic policies, and finite action spaces in the policy-gradient derivation (Proposition 1 relies on sums over actions), while experiments use continuous action spaces; the mismatch is not discussed.
The ablation story is thin: the claim that 'coupled resets' are essential is asserted empirically but not isolated in the presented results.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the Reach-Always-Avoid (RAA) and Reach-Reach (RR) problems generalize prior reach/avoid/reach-avoid HJ-RL formulations to dual-objective settings, and the paper convincingly argues (Fig. 2) why state augmentation is necessary.

Solid theoretical contribution: Theorems 1-3 and their supporting lemmas provide decomposition results (RAA into avoid + reach-avoid; RR into three reach problems) with detailed proofs in the supplementary material, including a non-trivial optimality result showing the proposed augmentation suffices over all history-dependent policies.

Practical algorithm: DO-HJ-PPO extends the SRBE-based PPO framework of [21] in a principled way, with a derived stochastic reach-avoid Bellman equation and corresponding policy gradient (Proposition 1), and reaches generalization of GAEs to the new Bellman operators.

Empirical results on continuous control tasks (Hopper, F16) show consistent improvements in success rate and steps-to-success over CPPO variants and an STL baseline, and the supplementary material provides reasonably complete hyperparameters and task definitions, supporting reproducibility.
Well-positioned related work distinguishing the approach from CMDPs, multi-objective RL, and temporal-logic RL.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core machinery (reach/avoid Bellman equations, discounted relaxations, the PPO-based actor-critic construction, GAE generalization) is directly inherited from [18, 19, 21]; the contribution is a relatively incremental composition of known operators rather than a new technique. The paper itself frames this as extending 'the list of solvable problems.'

Restrictive assumptions undermine practical significance: the theory assumes deterministic MDP dynamics, and the algorithm assumes access to the decomposed optimal values (V*A, V*R1, V*R2) which must themselves be learned; the relaxation to simultaneous learning is only empirically justified, and the impact of inexact decomposed values on the composed solution is not analyzed or ablated.

The state augmentation scales with the set of achievable reward/penalty values; for continuous rewards this augmentation is essentially continuous-dimensional history information, and how the practical algorithm handles this mismatch with the finite-value theory is not clearly explained.

Evaluation is narrow: only three environment families (grid-world, Hopper, F16), all with hand-crafted signed-distance rewards, and no standard safe-RL or multi-objective benchmarks. Baselines are somewhat ad hoc (three self-defined CPPO variants, a naive decomposed STL); comparisons with more established CMDP or max/min-objective methods would strengthen the claims. Statistical rigor (number of seeds, variance over runs, learning curves) is not reported in the main text.

Claims of 'less required tuning' and general superiority are stronger than the evidence; only 2-4 tasks per problem class are tested, and the worst-case 'equivalent at worst' statement is not quantitatively substantiated.

Presentation issues: several typos ('reach-aviod', 'solitons', 'incentive'), notation that is dense in places (e.g., the overloaded augmented-policy notation), and the main-text experiments rely heavily on figure-level results whose details are deferred to the supplementary material.

strengths: Clear and meaningful theoretical contribution: the paper generalizes existing HJ-RL value functions (Reach, Avoid, Reach-Avoid) to two new compositional problems (RAA, RR) and provides rigorous decomposition results (Theorems 1-2) with complete, detailed proofs in the appendix, including a carefully argued justification (Theorem 3) for why state augmentation with historical information is necessary and sufficient.

The discussion of the non-Markovian nature of the objectives and the contrast with temporal logic predicate algebra (Appendix L, including counterexamples showing TL-style decomposition fails at the value-function level) demonstrates conceptual depth and correct positioning against LTL/STL approaches.

Practical algorithm (DOHJ-PPO) is well-motivated, including design decisions like coupled resets, and comes with a policy-gradient result and stochastic (SRABE) relaxations with theoretical comparison results (Theorem 4).

Extensive empirical evaluation: 8 environment-task combinations, 10 baselines spanning Lagrangian/CMDP, HJ-RL, STL, and MORL approaches, evaluation over 1,000 trajectories per setting, plus an ablation on injected dynamics noise with multiple noise scales.
Reproducibility support is good: full hyperparameter tables for all environments, environment/reward definitions, and algorithmic details are provided.
The paper is honest about limitations, e.g., that expectation and extrema operators do not commute and guarantees under stochastic dynamics remain open.
weaknesses: The theory is developed only for deterministic, finite state/action MDPs, while the practical algorithm targets continuous control with stochasticity; the gap between the deterministic decomposition theorems and the stochastic relaxation used in DOHJ-PPO is handled empirically rather than with formal guarantees.

Experimental rigor has gaps: stochastic-dynamics ablations use only three seeds and plot the maximum learning curve over seeds, which can overstate performance; main results (Figure 4) also lack variance/confidence reporting, making the claimed dominance harder to verify statistically.

The RAA and RR problems are relatively narrow instantiations (min/max composition of two extremal objectives); the broader claim of a 'roadmap' to temporal-logic-style compositional specifications is deferred to future work without even preliminary results, limiting the perceived generality of the contribution.

Baselines require considerable adaptation (e.g., three ad-hoc CPPO variants in Appendix G) to fit these dual-objective tasks; the fairness and tuning budget of baselines relative to DOHJ-PPO ('little to no tuning' for the proposed method) is asserted but not systematically documented.

Notational/presentation issues undermine polish: a placeholder reference ('Prop. X in the Appendix'), typos ('Apendix', 'solitons', 'by anology', 'to incentive', 'amd' in Algorithm 1), and occasional notation inconsistencies (e.g., mangled maximums in Figure 1 image, r depending on either (x,y) or only x_PN in F16 rewards).

Novelty is moderate: the results are natural extensions of the SBE/RABE framework from Fisac et al. (2019), Hsu et al. (2021), and So et al. (2024), with the main intellectual contribution being the decomposition proofs; the impact, while real, is likely confined to the safe RL / HJ reachability sub-community.

strengths: The paper is technically solid: it extends the HJ-RL framework (SBE/RABE from Fisac et al. 2019, Hsu et al. 2021, So et al. 2024) to two new compositional problems (RAA and RR), and provides careful, non-trivial decomposition theorems (Theorems 1 and 2) with lengthy, detailed proofs in the appendix, including a formal argument for sufficiency of the proposed state augmentation (Theorem 3).

The evaluation is comparatively broad for this sub-area: DOHJ-PPO is compared against ten baselines spanning Lagrangian methods, HJ-RL methods, and STL/MORL-based PPO variants, across four continuous-control environments and two task types, with evaluation on 1,000 trajectories and an additional stochastic-dynamics ablation.

The qualitative grid-world demonstration (Figure 2) nicely illustrates why the RAA/RR values induce different behaviors than the simpler RA/R formulations, and the appendix discussion contrasting value-function decomposition with temporal-logic quantitative-semantics decomposition (Appendix L) is a thoughtful clarification that preempts a likely reviewer objection.
The proposed algorithm is a reasonably principled adaptation of PPO (SRABE, HJ-GAE, coupled resets) rather than an ad hoc heuristic, and the ablation on coupled resets is mentioned.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental. The core machinery (SBE, RABE, discounting tricks, PPO adaptation, GAE generalization) is directly inherited from Hsu et al. (2021) and So et al. (2024); the new contribution is essentially showing that two new min/max compositions admit decompositions into previously studied problems. This is a natural next step, and the theoretical difficulty, while real, is not substantial for a top-tier venue.

The problem class addressed is narrow. RAA and RR are two specific dual-objective compositions; the paper acknowledges that extending to general temporal-logic compositions would require 'generalized decomposition principles for nontrivial compositions of logical operations' that are left to future work. As is, the contribution is limited to two special cases, which limits the significance and generality of the results.

The stochastic-dynamics story is weak theoretically. The SRABE simply swaps extrema and expectation operators, which the authors admit do not commute; no guarantee is provided for the stochastic case beyond an 'artificial ablation' on HalfCheetah only. The theoretical validity of the method under exactly the conditions where RL is actually used (stochastic policies, noise) is therefore not established.

Evaluation rigor concerns: Figure 5 plots the maximum learning curve over only three seeds, which inflates apparent performance and masks variance; the stochastic ablation is limited to a single environment; and success/partial-success metrics, while sensible, are coarse and environment-specific. Claims of 'little to no tuning' are undermined by extensive per-environment hyperparameter tables (learning rates, gamma annealing schedules, entropy coefficients differ across all four environments), and baseline hyperparameters (e.g., CPPO's KP=1 vs KP=100) appear inconsistently tuned.

Writing quality issues reduce confidence: dangling references ('Prop. X in the Appendix'), typos ('by anology', 'Apendix', 'solitons', 'HO P P E R'), an inconsistent Theorem 4 proof outline, and several garbled formula renderings. These suggest the manuscript was not carefully prepared.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no code release is mentioned despite the algorithm having multiple interacting components (composed/decomposed critics, coupled resets, HJ-GAEs) whose exact implementation details materially affect results, and the ablation on coupled resets is asserted empirically rather than shown with figures or numbers.

strengths: The paper extends the HJ-RL framework (SBE/RABE of Fisac et al. 2019 and Hsu et al. 2021) to two genuinely new compositional problems (RAA and RR) that go beyond the existing Reach/Avoid/Reach-Avoid repertoire, and the resulting value functions have a clean, direct interpretation as hard-constraint satisfaction.

The theoretical contribution is substantial and carefully done: Theorems 1-3 (with lengthy, detailed proofs in the appendix) rigorously establish that the RAA and RR optimal values and policies decompose into combinations of previously studied reach, avoid, and reach-avoid value functions, and that the proposed state augmentation is sufficient (no further history can help). The appendix also includes a useful discussion distinguishing these decompositions from temporal-logic predicate algebra.

DOHJ-PPO is a principled algorithm derived from the theory (stochastic SRBE/SRABE relaxations, coupled resets, bootstrapped decomposed critics), with a policy-gradient proposition and contractive discounted forms provided.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: four continuous-control environments, a broad set of ~10 baselines spanning Lagrangian, HJ-RL, STL, and MORL approaches, evaluation over 1,000 trajectories, success/partial-success/time-to-success metrics, and a controlled noise-ablation study on stochastic dynamics.
The manuscript is well organized, clearly written, and honest about limitations (non-commutativity of expectation and extrema, lack of guarantees under stochastic dynamics).
weaknesses: The contribution, while solid, is a fairly natural next step in a specific line of work (Hsu et al. 2021; So et al. 2024; So and Fan 2023); the RAA/RR problems are special cases of STL conjunction specifications, and the paper's positioning against the LTL/STL literature is acknowledged but the practical scope remains limited to two specific two-objective compositions.

The theoretical results are derived for finite, deterministic MDPs; the algorithmic extension to stochastic settings (SRABE) interchanges expectation and extremal operators without formal guarantees, and this gap is only empirically (not theoretically) addressed.

DOHJ-PPO contains several heuristic design choices (coupled resets, concurrent bootstrapping of decomposed and composed critics) whose benefits are argued mainly empirically; only an informal ablation (omitting coupled resets) is reported, and no systematic ablation of the other components is provided.

In Figure 5 the reported curves are the maximum over three seeds, which can overstate performance; seed variance for the main results is not clearly reported, and several figures (e.g., Figure 4 bar charts) are difficult to read at the provided resolution.

No explicit statement of code release or reproducibility artifacts is provided in the main text, which is a concern for a paper whose evaluation involves many bespoke baselines and environment modifications.

Some presentation issues remain (e.g., 'Prop. X in the Appendix' placeholder-style reference on page 7, typos such as 'anology', 'Apendix', 'solitons'), suggesting the manuscript is not fully polished.
